sections.title: have to, don’t have to, must, mustn’t

reference.title: have to, don’t have to
rows: I have to speak English at work. She has to get up at seven every day.
We don’t have to wear a uniform at this school. He doesn’t have to work on Saturdays.
Do I have to buy a grammar book? What time does she have to get up in the morning?

reference.title: must, mustn’t
rows: You must do your homework tonight. She must tidy her room before she goes out.
You mustn’t leave your bags here. I mustn’t forget to call her tonight. (mustn’t = must not)
Must I go to bed now? When must we decide about the party?

reference.title: have to / don’t have to
reference.text: have to + infinitive = rules and obligations. don’t have to + infinitive = there is no obligation, it isn’t necessary. Use do / does in questions and negatives: Do I have to go? NOT Have I to go? Don’t contract have or has: I have to go. NOT I’ve to go.

reference.title: must / mustn’t
reference.text: must / mustn’t + infinitive without to. They are the same for all persons (he must, not he musts). mustn’t = something is prohibited.

reference.title: must and have to
reference.text: They are very similar. We normally use have to for a general obligation (a rule at work / school or a law): We have to start work at seven. We normally use must for a personal obligation (one that the speaker imposes): You must go to bed now! But often we can use either.

reference.title: mustn’t and don’t have to
reference.text: They have completely different meanings. You mustn’t go. = It’s prohibited. Don’t go. You don’t have to go. = You can go if you want to, but it isn’t necessary.

reference.title: Impersonal you
reference.text: We often use have to and must with you = people in general: You have to wear a seatbelt in a car. You mustn’t take photos in the museum.

reference.wrong: You don’t have to smoke here. (It’s prohibited.)
reference.why: Prohibited = mustn’t. don’t have to = not necessary.

reference.wrong: She must to wear a uniform.
reference.right: She must wear a uniform. / She has to wear a uniform.
reference.why: must + infinitive without to; have to / has to + infinitive.

reference.title: Stress on prepositions
reference.text: Prepositions are usually unstressed: I’m good at /ət/ tennis. Sugar is bad for /fə/ your teeth. But when a preposition comes at the end of a question or sentence, it is stressed and has its strong form: What are you interested in? What’s she famous for /fɔː/?

tasks.instruction: Read the article Are the British really so bad at learning languages? Put the topic sentences in the order of the paragraphs 1–6
tasks.note: SB 2b → Order: карточки A–F по порядку абзацев 1–6 (1 E — пример в книге, оставлен в порядке)
tasks.context:
1 ___ That’s been true for a long time. In any city around the world you can hear British tourists asking for the restaurant menu in English. Sometimes they try to say a couple of phrases in the local language, but they stop making an effort as soon as they discover that the waiter knows a little English. Some British people who live abroad often spend all their time with other Brits, and never learn the language at all.
2 ___ Many British people think ‘I don’t have to learn a foreign language because everyone speaks English nowadays’. This is partly true. In many multinational companies, for example, employees have to speak English as it is the company’s official language of communication.
3 ___ Children only have to learn a language until they are 14. After that, they don’t have to continue if they don’t want to. Thirty per cent of young people say that they don’t want to carry on with a foreign language because ‘it’s too difficult’.
4 ___ A newspaper decided to find out by sending Max, one of its journalists, on an intensive language course. He then had to go to the country and do some ‘tests’ to see if he could ‘survive’ in different situations.
5 ___ ‘I’d like to visit Spain and Latin America in the future. If I go, I don’t want to be the typical Brit who expects everyone else to speak English.’ He did a one-month intensive course at a language school in London.
6 ___ When his course finished he went to Madrid for the weekend to do his tests. A teacher called Paula met him there and gave him a mark out of ten for each test and then a final mark for everything.

tasks.instruction: Write a formal email to Dublin English First asking for information. Write two paragraphs
tasks.context: Learn English in Dublin. Come and improve your English this summer! We run courses from two to four weeks. You can have classes from three to six hours a day or you can combine studying with cultural activities like theatre trips or museum visits. There are General English courses from Beginner to Advanced, as well as Business English and exam preparation classes. You can stay with a local family, or in student accommodation. Write to us for more information. Tell us about yourself and what you are looking for, and we will suggest the perfect course for you.

exercises.prompt: Write a formal email to the school. Decide how long you want to study for, what kind of course, and where you want to stay. Ask two or three questions.

questions.text: Paragraph 1: Why are you writing? Give some personal information (your age, occupation, and your level of English).
questions.hint: (Dear Sir / Madam, I am writing to ask for information about… I am … years old and I…)

questions.text: Paragraph 2: What would you like to do? Ask your questions and ask them to send you the information.
questions.hint: (I would like to… Is it possible to…? Could you please send me…?)

questions.text: How do you finish the email?
questions.hint: (I look forward to hearing from you. Yours faithfully,)

criteria: starts with Dear Sir / Madam and ends with I look forward to hearing from you. Yours faithfully,
two paragraphs: personal information, then the course and questions
formal style: no contractions (I am, I would like), however instead of but
at least two polite questions (Is it possible to…? Could you please…?)

sections.title: Episode 4 · At the pharmacy
sections.note: Rob and Jenny go running in Central Park. The next day Rob isn’t feeling well and goes to a pharmacy. In the evening he has dinner at Jenny’s apartment.

reference.title: Going to a pharmacy
rows: Good morning. Can I help you?
I’m not feeling very well. I think I have flu.
I have a headache and a cough.
Are you allergic to any drugs?
No problem. This is ibuprofen. It’ll make you feel better.
How many do I have to take?
Two every four hours. If you don’t feel better in 48 hours, you should see a doctor.
OK, thanks. How much is that?

reference.title: have got
reference.text: We sometimes use have got instead of have to talk about possession. I’ve got a busy day tomorrow. Have you got any children? Yes, I have. I’ve got a girl and a boy. / No, I haven’t. I haven’t got children.

reference.title: British and American English
reference.text: pharmacy = American English (and sometimes British English); chemist’s = British English. drugs = medicine in American English; drugs = illegal substances in British and American English.

reference.title: Social English
rows: That isn’t very good for you.
I think I should get back to the hotel now.
Thanks again for a great evening.
